transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi… um, I’m here because flying has started feeling way scarier than I think it should. Like, even just thinking about getting on a plane now, my mind immediately goes back to this really awful turbulence we had on my honeymoon flight. I know, logically, people fly safely all the time—like I can tell myself the statistics and all that—but it doesn’t seem to calm the part of me that just pictures being back there again.
When you think about getting on a plane and picture that turbulence, do you ever feel like you're having a panic attack?

I think… maybe, yes, or at least it feels like the beginning of one. Like if I’m looking up flights for a conference, even before I’ve booked anything, my chest tightens right away. It’s almost instant, like my body reacts before I’ve even had a chance to talk myself through it.

And it’s not only when I’m actively planning to fly. Sometimes if I hear a plane overhead, I get this sudden rush of panic, like I need to stop what I’m doing or get away from the thought. With the flight searches, I’ll literally want to shut the laptop, like closing the page will make the feeling stop. So I don’t know if that counts as a full panic attack, but it feels like this immediate wave of fear that just hits me.
Do you experience this kind of fear or panic in situations other than flying?

Not really… I mean, I get stressed about normal things, but this kind of fear is really tied to flying. It’s specifically the idea of being on a plane that sets it off. Like even just imagining boarding or sitting there and then hitting turbulence makes me go right back to that honeymoon flight in my head.

And I know that probably sounds kind of irrational because, logically, I do know people fly safely every day. I can say that to myself, and I do say it to myself, but it doesn’t really change how scared I feel when I picture getting on a plane. So no, I don’t think I have this same kind of panic in other situations—it’s really flying.
How long have you been experiencing this fear of flying?

It’s been… a little over two years now. It started after that flight back from my honeymoon—the one with the really bad turbulence. That was about two years and five months ago, I think. I didn’t really think at first it would turn into this ongoing thing, because I figured maybe I was just shaken up and it would fade, but it’s kind of stayed with me since then.
Has this fear of flying stopped you from taking any trips or traveling somewhere you wanted to go?

Yes… it has. I’m still functioning day to day, like I go to work, I handle things at home, I’m not completely shut down or anything like that. But it’s definitely started changing what I say yes to.

At work, there have been trainings and conferences that my supervisor really thought would be good for me—like the kind of things that would help me grow or make connections—and if they involve flying, I find reasons not to go. I’ll tell myself it’s not the right time, or that someone else would benefit more, but really it’s because I don’t want to get on a plane.

And personally, too… there was a trip to Florence I had been really excited about, and it just keeps getting pushed back. I haven’t fully canceled the idea, but I keep avoiding actually planning it because as soon as it becomes real, then I’d have to deal with flying there. So, yes, it hasn’t ruined my whole life, but it is definitely limiting things I wanted to do.
Have you avoided any other activities or situations because they might involve flying, aside from work conferences and the trip to Florence?

Yes, mostly anything where flying is part of it or might become part of it. Like, I’ve started automatically looking for ways to avoid the plane part before I even decide if I want to do something.

If there’s a place we could technically drive to, even if it’s a really long drive, I’ll push for that instead. I’ll say, “Oh, it might be nice to see things along the way,” or “We can make a road trip out of it,” and sometimes that’s partly true, but really it’s because driving feels like an escape from having to fly. I know it can be inconvenient and take way more time, but I still choose it if it means I don’t have to get on a plane.

And with work, it’s not just the bigger conferences I mentioned. Even smaller trainings or professional things, if I hear they’re out of state and flying would be expected, I kind of shut down on the idea right away. I’ll avoid volunteering, or I’ll wait too long to respond, or I’ll make it sound like my schedule is the issue.

Even just talking seriously about a trip can be hard. If I absolutely have to discuss plans, like dates or flights or whether we’re really going, I need my husband sitting with me. Not because he fixes it exactly, but because if he’s not there, I’ll start backing out or changing the subject or finding reasons to postpone it. With him there, I can at least get through the conversation.
Has your fear of flying affected your relationships with friends or family in any way?

A little, yes… not in a dramatic way where people are angry at me all the time or anything, but it has created some tension. Mostly with my husband, because he’s the one who sees how much I avoid making decisions around travel. Like with the Florence trip, we were both excited about it, and I keep saying, “Yes, we’ll do it, we’ll figure it out,” but then when it comes time to actually look at dates or flights, I sort of stall. I can tell that’s frustrating for him, even though he tries to be patient.

With family or friends, it’s more that I’ve become less flexible. If someone talks about a trip or an event that would require flying, I’m already thinking of reasons why it might not work. And I don’t always say, “It’s because I’m scared to fly,” so I think sometimes it probably comes across like I’m not interested or I’m being difficult.

I’m still managing my normal life—work, home, day-to-day stuff—but I can see how it’s narrowing what I’m willing to do. I pass up work trainings and conferences that my supervisor thinks would be good for me, and then personally I keep pushing back plans I actually want, like Florence. So relationships haven’t fallen apart, but it does affect how available I am for things.
Are there any parts of your daily routine or activities, not related to travel, where you feel your fear of flying is affecting your behavior or decisions?

Not really, no… at least not that I’ve noticed in a clear way. My regular day-to-day routine is pretty normal. I go to work, I do the things I need to do at home, run errands, see people, that kind of thing. It’s not like I’m avoiding normal places or changing my schedule because of it.

It mostly shows up when something connects to the idea of flying or travel planning. If it’s not related to that, I don’t think it affects my decisions much. I mean, I might be a little more aware of it in the background if someone randomly brings up a vacation or an airport or something, but in terms of my daily behavior… no, I don’t think it really changes what I do.
Would you say that your fear of flying is causing you a lot of distress or anxiety most of the time?

I wouldn’t say it’s constant, like I’m anxious every hour of every day, but when flying comes up, yes, it really does distress me. That’s honestly why I’m here. It feels like flying has become way scarier in my head than it probably should be.

Even just the idea of getting on a plane can make me immediately picture that turbulence from my honeymoon flight again. It’s like my mind goes right back there, even though another part of me knows people fly safely every day and that turbulence doesn’t automatically mean something terrible is going to happen. I can tell myself that logically, but it doesn’t really calm the reaction down very much.

So, not “most of the time” in my normal daily life, but most of the time when flying is even a possibility, it causes a lot of anxiety.
Have you ever considered seeking help or treatment specifically for your fear of flying before coming here today?

I don’t think I really did, not in any serious or organized way. I mean, I’ve thought things like, “Maybe I should talk to someone about this,” especially when a trip comes up and I can feel myself getting worked up, but I didn’t actually follow through before now.

Part of it was that I kept telling myself it wasn’t a big enough problem, because I can get through everyday life fine as long as I’m not dealing with planes. And part of it was probably embarrassment, honestly. Like, it feels a little silly to say out loud that I’m this afraid of something that so many people do all the time. So I mostly just avoided it or tried to reason with myself instead of getting help.

Coming here is really the first time I’ve taken it seriously enough to actually talk to a professional about it.
Have you ever avoided a significant life event, like a wedding or a family reunion, because it would have required flying?

I haven’t missed something like a wedding or a family reunion, no… not something that major, at least not yet. But I have definitely changed what I agree to do because of it.

Like, I’ve chosen really long drives instead of flying, even when flying would have made way more sense. I’ll tell myself, “Oh, it’s fine, we can just drive,” but honestly it’s because the idea of the airport and the plane feels like too much. And with work, I’ve turned down trainings before if they were far enough away that flying would be expected. I kind of make it sound practical, like scheduling or cost or being busy, but underneath it’s really that I don’t want to have to get on a plane.

And even just talking about a possible trip can be hard. If it gets to the point where we’re actually discussing details, I usually need my husband sitting there with me, because otherwise I start wanting to shut it down or back out before anything is decided. So, not a huge family event, but it has affected choices that matter.
Have you ever felt like your fear of flying has prevented you from achieving a personal or professional goal that was important to you?

Yes… I think it has, though I feel a little uncomfortable saying that because I’m still functioning, you know? I’m still going to work, I’m still taking care of things at home, so it’s not like my whole life has stopped. But it has started narrowing what I’m willing to do.

Professionally, the biggest thing is trainings and conferences. My supervisor has mentioned a few that she thought would be good for me, like things that could help me grow in my role or maybe open up more opportunities later. And if they’re local, I’m fine. But when they’re far enough away that flying would make the most sense, I immediately start finding reasons not to go. I’ll say it’s not a good time, or that maybe someone else should attend, or that I have too much going on. But honestly, the flying part is a huge reason.

And personally, there’s this trip to Florence that I had been really excited about. It wasn’t just some random vacation idea — it felt like one of those things I really wanted to do, something I kept imagining and talking about. But it keeps getting pushed back because once it becomes real and we’d actually have to book flights, I freeze up. So, yes, I wouldn’t say it has ruined my life or anything, but it has definitely gotten in the way of things that matter to me.
Have you ever felt like your fear of flying has caused you to avoid something you really wanted to do to the point where you felt you were missing out on something significant?

Yes… I think that’s probably the part that bothers me the most, honestly. I wouldn’t say my life has fallen apart or anything — I’m still managing my job, I’m still doing what I need to do at home, I get through my day-to-day responsibilities. So sometimes I convince myself it’s not that serious.

But then I look at the things I’ve passed up, and it does feel like I’m missing out. With work, for example, there have been trainings and conferences my supervisor thought would be really useful for me, like things that could help me grow or be seen as more capable in my role. And instead of thinking, “That sounds good,” my mind goes straight to whether I’d have to fly. If the answer is yes, I start backing away from it, or I come up with another reason why it’s not the right time.

And personally, the Florence trip is the big one. I was really excited about it — like genuinely excited, not just casually interested. I’d imagined going, talked about it, looked forward to it. But every time it gets close to actually making plans and booking flights, I kind of stall. So it keeps getting pushed back, and then I feel sad and frustrated with myself because it feels like I’m letting this one fear make my life smaller than I want it to be.
